facet_contributions.boundaries: Findings are inconsistent across tumor types (e.g., Akkermansia showed decreased levels in one prostate cancer study). Correlations do not prove causation. Sample sizes vary widely. Probiotic effects are highly strain-specific and sometimes detrimental.
facet_contributions.contribution: Summarizes observational data linking specific microbial abundances (e.g., high Akkermansia/Bifidobacterium) to improved ICI response in solid tumors. Details the negative association between antibiotic use and ICI efficacy. Provides evidence for FMT restoring sensitivity in a subset of patients.
facet_contributions.possible_uses: Use to illustrate the current state of biomarker discovery for ICI response prediction. Use to discuss the clinical reality of antibiotic stewardship in oncology. Use to contextualize the experimental nature of FMT and probiotic therapies.

facet_contributions.boundaries: Mechanisms are often derived from animal models or in vitro studies. Human translation is not fully confirmed. Conflicting roles of metabolites (e.g., butyrate enhancing CD8+ T cells vs. increasing Tregs). The 'precise mechanism' is explicitly stated as unclear in the text.
facet_contributions.contribution: Describes proposed mechanisms: microbiota-derived metabolites (SCFAs, PSA) modulating immune cell function (Treg/Th17 differentiation, cytokine production). Explains how microbiota maintains intestinal homeostasis and influences systemic immunity. Mentions direct tumor effects (apoptosis induction, pathway activation).
facet_contributions.possible_uses: Use to outline the hypothesized biological pathways connecting gut flora to immune checkpoint blockade. Highlight the complexity and potential contradictions in mechanistic understanding (e.g., dual roles of SCFAs).

paper_identity.title: Gut microbiota influences the efficiency of immune checkpoint inhibitors by modulating the immune system (Review)

planning_summary: This review serves as a foundational source for mapping the landscape of gut microbiome-ICI interactions. It provides a structured overview of candidate microbial taxa, metabolites, and clinical interventions (antibiotics, probiotics, FMT) relevant to both efficacy and toxicity (irAEs). Crucially, it highlights the heterogeneity of results across tumor types and the current lack of consensus on specific mechanisms, offering valuable context for discussing why microbiome modulation strategies have yielded variable clinical outcomes.
scope_interpretation_cautions: The review covers multiple tumor types, not just solid tumors exclusively, though most examples are solid tumors. Be cautious when generalizing findings to specific cancers.
Many mechanistic claims are based on animal or in vitro studies; human validation is often lacking or preliminary.
The term 'gut microbiota' includes bacteria, archaea, fungi, and viruses, but the review focuses predominantly on bacteria.
Conflicting results within the same review (e.g., regarding butyrate or probiotics) must be preserved to reflect the uncertainty in the field.
topic_handles: Candidate microbial taxa (Akkermansia muciniphila, Bifidobacterium, Faecalibacterium, Ruminococcus)
Microbial metabolites (SCFAs: butyrate, propionate; bile acids)
Immune modulation mechanisms (Th17/Treg balance, IL-10, IFN-gamma)
Clinical interventions (Antibiotics usage, Probiotic supplementation, Fecal Microbiota Transplantation)
Adverse events (Immune-related adverse events: irAEs, colitis)
Tumor type specificity (Melanoma vs. NSCLC vs. Colorectal Cancer vs. HCC)
